We're migrating 40 staff from our old CRM to a new one over a single weekend. Give me the plan.

**Weekend CRM migration plan (40 staff):**

1. **Friday 18:00 — freeze.** Old CRM goes read-only; announce it twice (email + standup). Export the full dataset and checksum it.
2. **Friday night — dry run.** Load the export into the new CRM's sandbox, run the field-mapping script, and diff record counts per object (accounts, contacts, deals). Any object off by more than 0.1% stops the line.
3. **Saturday — real load.** Import in dependency order, then run the same count diff against production. Spot-check 20 records by hand, including the 5 most complex accounts.
4. **Sunday — people.** All 40 staff log in, reset passwords, and complete a 20-minute checklist (find a contact, log a call, create a deal). Two floor-walkers handle lockouts.
5. **Monday 08:00 — go/no-go.** If the checklist pass rate is above 90% and counts reconcile, the old CRM stays read-only as the fallback for two weeks, then is archived.

The single biggest risk is not the data, it is Monday-morning password chaos — that is why the Sunday login drill is in the plan.

We need to clean up a shared drive with about 9,000 files before an audit in six weeks. Plan it.

**Shared drive cleanup plan (9,000 files, 6 weeks to audit):**

1. **Week 1 — inventory, no deleting.** Generate a full listing with owner, size, and last-modified date. Auditors forgive mess; they do not forgive missing evidence, so nothing is deleted before the inventory exists.
2. **Week 2 — classify.** Bucket files into keep / archive / delete candidates by rule: untouched for 3+ years and no legal-hold tag goes to archive candidates; true duplicates (same hash) go to delete candidates.
3. **Weeks 3-4 — owner review.** Each folder owner gets their bucket list and two weeks to object. Silence counts as consent, stated in writing up front.
4. **Week 5 — execute.** Archive first, delete second, in that order, with the inventory snapshot preserved.
5. **Week 6 — buffer and report.** Write the one-page summary the auditors will actually read: what existed, what moved, what was deleted and under whose approval.

Expected outcome: roughly 30-40% of a drive that size is usually archivable, which is what makes the remaining structure auditable.

- **Days 3-4:** Docs and help article written from the changelog; support team gets a 30-minute walkthrough and the three questions customers will ask first.
- **Day 5:** Release notes and announcement email drafted. Legal/privacy check if the feature touches user data.
- **Days 6-7:** Ship to 5% of users. Watch error rates and support contacts against the pre-launch baseline, with a named person owning the kill switch.
- **Day 8:** If metrics are clean, go to 50%. If not, you still have two days of buffer — use them, that is what they are for.
- **Day 9:** Full rollout.
- **Day 10:** Announcement goes out, one day after the feature is already live and proven, so the announcement never promises something that is still breaking.
We're hosting a hiring event for 6 roles with about 80 candidates in one afternoon. Plan it.

**Hiring event plan (6 roles, ~80 candidates, one afternoon):**

**Structure:** 13-14 candidates per role. Run 20-minute structured interviews in parallel rooms: 6 rooms, one per role, two interviewers per room so scoring is never one person's impression.

**Flow:** Candidates check in, get a badge with their time slots, and rotate: interview (20 min), a short work-sample task (25 min), and a team culture conversation (15 min). Stagger starts every 10 minutes so rooms never bottleneck.

**Scoring:** Same rubric for every candidate for a role, scored in the room before the next candidate enters — end-of-day scoring from memory is how bias gets in.

**Close:** Interviewers meet for 45 minutes the same evening to rank their top 3 per role while impressions are fresh. Every candidate hears back within 5 business days, including the noes; silence is the thing candidates remember and repeat.
Plan how to reconcile a year of messy expense receipts before tax season.

**Expense receipt reconciliation plan:**

1. **Gather once.** Pull every source in one pass: email receipts, the card statement export, the shared folder, and the shoebox. Photograph paper receipts the day you touch them.
2. **Match by amount and date.** Most receipts match a statement line on amount alone; date within 3 days breaks ties. Expect about 80% to match automatically or by inspection.
3. **Quarantine the rest.** Unmatched statement lines and orphan receipts go on one exception list. Work it in one sitting with the cardholder, not in drips over weeks.
4. **Categorize as you match**, not after — recategorizing 12 months at the end doubles the work.
5. **Write the gaps down.** Missing receipts get a short signed note (date, amount, purpose) while memory is fresh; accountants accept documented gaps far better than reconstructed paperwork.

Realistic pace: a year of small-business expenses is two focused days, not the month people fear.
Give me a plan for a quarterly data-quality audit of our customer database.

**Quarterly data-quality audit plan:**

**Sample, don't census.** Pull a random 500 records plus every record created by bulk import. Check five fields that matter (email, phone, company, status, owner) for completeness, validity, and duplication.

**Measure four things:** duplicate rate (fuzzy match on name+email), dead-email rate, records with no owner, and status values outside the allowed list. Compare each against last quarter — the trend is the audit, not the snapshot.

**Find the source, not just the errors.** Every error class usually traces to one intake path: a form without validation, an import template, an integration. Fix the top two sources and the error rate drops permanently; fixing records alone rents the improvement for one quarter.

**Report on one page:** the four metrics, the trend arrows, the two sources fixed, and the two targeted next quarter.
Plan a research sprint: we have five days to decide whether to enter a new market.

**Five-day market-entry research sprint:**

- **Day 1 — frame.** Write the decision as one sentence and list the five facts that would change it. If a fact would not change the decision, it is not research, it is decoration.
- **Day 2 — desk research.** Market size from two independent sources, and they must be reconciled if they disagree — an unreconciled pair of numbers is how bad entries happen. Competitor pricing scraped from public pages, not brochures.
- **Day 3 — customers.** 8-10 interviews with buyers in that market, recruited before the sprint starts. Ask about their current workaround and what it costs them; that is your real price ceiling.
- **Day 4 — economics.** Build the unit model with the interview data: acquisition cost, realistic price, delivery cost. Kill criteria written before the model is run.
- **Day 5 — decide.** One memo: enter, don't enter, or the single experiment that would settle it, with an owner and a date.

The sprint fails if it ends with 'more research needed' and no experiment named.
We need to schedule a maintenance window for a system used in 9 countries. Plan how to pick and announce it.

**Maintenance window plan (users in 9 countries):**

**Pick the window from data, not habit.** Pull hourly usage for the last 30 days per country and find the global trough — for a 9-country spread it usually lands around 02:00-05:00 UTC, but verify; a 'quiet' window that is 9am in your largest market is a career event.

**Sequence:** Announce 14 days out, remind at 7 days and 24 hours, in each region's local time and language. State the window as start-end with the timezone spelled out, never as a bare '2am'.

**During:** Status page updated at start, midpoint, and completion — silence during a window reads as a failure. A named engineer owns the abort decision with pre-agreed criteria (if step 3 of 7 is not done by the midpoint, roll back).

**After:** Post the actual duration vs planned, and what, if anything, was deferred to the next window.
Plan a travel itinerary for a 3-city, 4-day business trip with tight connections.

**3-city, 4-day itinerary plan:**

**Routing rule:** Order the cities geographically, not by meeting importance, and put the most important meeting on day 2 — day 1 carries the travel-delay risk, and day 4 carries the get-home pressure.

**Connections:** Minimum 90 minutes between flights on separate tickets, 60 on one ticket. Never book the last flight of the day into a city where you have a morning meeting; the cost of one hotel night beats the cost of a missed meeting by an order of magnitude.

**Daily shape:** Day 1 travel + one light meeting max. Day 2 the anchor meeting + one more. Day 3 second city meetings. Day 4 final city by noon, home by evening.

**Buffers and backups:** Screenshot every boarding pass, keep the next-best alternative flight for each leg noted in the itinerary, and put one phone number — the travel booker's, not an app — at the top of the document.
Give me a plan to run a vendor security review for a new SaaS tool in two weeks.

**Two-week SaaS security review plan:**

**Days 1-2 — scope.** What data will the tool hold, whose accounts connect to it, and what happens to us if it leaks? The review's depth follows the data classification, not the vendor's size.

**Days 3-5 — evidence.** Request: SOC 2 report (read the exceptions section, not the cover), penetration test summary and date, sub-processor list, data retention and deletion terms, and breach notification SLA. A vendor that cannot produce a SOC 2 gets the enhanced questionnaire instead — slower, and that is their problem, not yours.

**Days 6-8 — technical checks.** SSO/SAML support, SCIM provisioning, audit log export, encryption in transit and at rest, and whether your data trains their models — get that answer in writing.

**Days 9-10 — decide.** Written verdict: approve, approve with conditions (e.g., no production data until DPA is signed), or reject, each with the evidence cited. File the evidence with the verdict; next year's review starts from it.
Plan how to onboard a remote employee across 6 time zones of team spread.

**Remote onboarding plan (team spread across 6 time zones):**

**Week 0, before day 1:** Accounts created, hardware shipped and confirmed working, and a buddy assigned in an adjacent time zone (within 3 hours) — a buddy 9 hours away is a pen pal, not a buddy.

**Week 1:** Two live anchors per day maximum, placed in the overlap window; everything else async with recordings. Day 1 is for introductions and access checks, not information transfer. Their first real task ships by day 3 — small, real, and reviewable.

**Weeks 2-4:** A written 30-60-90 with the manager, reviewed live once a week at a time that rotates so the same person is not always taking the 7am slot.

**The thing most plans miss:** a map of who knows what, with time zones on it, so the new hire knows who they can ask right now versus who answers tomorrow.
We want to run a price test on our website for two weeks. Plan it properly.

**Two-week price test plan:**

**Design:** Randomize at the visitor level, 50/50, one price variable only — testing price and page copy together tells you nothing about either. Exclude existing customers in negotiation; a prospect finding two prices is a trust incident, so the test runs on new-visitor traffic only.

**Power first:** Compute the sample size from your baseline conversion rate and the smallest lift worth acting on (say 10% relative) before launching. If two weeks of traffic cannot reach it, extend the window now rather than reading tea leaves later.

**Guardrails:** Pre-register the decision rule (adopt if conversion-adjusted revenue per visitor rises and refund rate does not), the stop rule (pause if complaints or refund rate spike), and the analysis date.

**After:** Announce the result internally either way. A killed test with a written result is a success; a quiet one gets repeated by another team next year.
Plan a documentation cleanup for a wiki that has grown to about 2,000 pages.

**Wiki cleanup plan (2,000 pages):**

1. **Measure first.** Export page metadata: owner, last edit, view count. Pages sort themselves into obvious buckets once you can see age and traffic together.
2. **Buckets:** Keep (edited or viewed in 6 months), Archive (not viewed in a year, no owner), Merge (duplicate topics — expect 10-15% of a wiki this size), and Fix (high traffic, stale content — these are your most dangerous pages, because people trust them).
3. **Order of work:** Fix the stale high-traffic pages first, merge duplicates second, archive last. Archiving is satisfying and low-value; accuracy on the pages everyone reads is the opposite.
4. **Prevent regrowth:** Every new page gets an owner and a review date at creation, and search gets a 'last verified' stamp. Without this, you are scheduling the same cleanup for next year.
